strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether autoencoding pretraining is necessary for trainable context compression. The paper provides direct empirical evidence (Table 5) that removing the AE objective can help, which is a useful finding for the community.
The method is simple, well-specified, and training-efficient (~26-31% faster pretraining than baselines with lower LM perplexity, Table 7).

Reasonably comprehensive experiments: in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA evaluation across three compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), with retraining of all soft-compression baselines on the same data for fair comparison.

Thorough ablation studies covering the two architectural components (anchor embedding, bidirectional attention), token selection strategies (random, Lingua-2, uniform), and the AE objective, with full per-dataset results in the appendix.
Qualitative analyses (attention maps, t-SNE of key/value spaces, training curves) support the claim that anchor-token representations stay closer to the original context token distribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: SAC is essentially a combination of existing ideas — trainable KV-based compression (500xCompressor), uniform position-aware token selection (EPL), and bidirectional attention for encoder-style use of decoder LLMs (LLM2Vec/NV-Embed). The individual components and their motivations are largely known.

Narrow evaluation scope: only Llama-3.2-1B as both encoder and target LLM, and only MRQA-style extractive QA. No long-context benchmarks (e.g., LongBench, needle-in-a-haystack, summarization), no larger models, and contexts are chunked into 510-token sub-contexts, which weakens the central claim of accelerating long-context LLM inference.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (EPL) are modest at 5x compression (~0.7-1.0 average F1/EM points) and results are mixed per-dataset (e.g., SAC underperforms EPL on BioASQ at 5x OOD), so the 'consistently outperforms' claim is stronger than the evidence; no statistical significance tests or multiple seeds are reported.

The core hypothesis (anchor tokens are inherently easier for the target LLM to understand) is supported only by qualitative visualization; no quantitative measure of representation alignment or causal analysis is provided.

Anchor selection is trivial (middle token of each chunk) and the ablation shows Lingua-2 selection performs nearly identically, leaving the 'semantic anchor' framing somewhat overstated; the architecture, not the selection, drives the gains.
Reproducibility concerns: the anonymous code link in the reproducibility statement appears to be missing/blank, and there are minor writing issues (e.g., 'inferenece', incomplete sentence).
Hyperparameters (LoRA rank 128, fixed 20k steps) and how sensitive results are to these choices are not explored; only the default configuration is reported.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written: the identified mismatch between autoencoding-based compression training and downstream task usage is a legitimate and interesting observation about ICAE-style methods.

The proposed method is simple and coherent: deriving compressed representations from context tokens themselves (anchor tokens), adding learned anchor embeddings, and using bidirectional attention during compression are sensible design choices that avoid costly AE pretraining.

The experimental evaluation is fairly comprehensive for its scope: in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA evaluation, three compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), comparison against recent baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, LLMLingua-2) trained on the same data, and multiple ablations (components, token selection strategies, AE objective effects).

The analysis sections (attention map visualization, t-SNE of Key/Value representation spaces, pretraining perplexity and training-time comparison) provide some mechanistic insight into why anchor-token-based representations behave differently from learned compression tokens.
Hyperparameters, training details, and full per-dataset ablation results are provided, and the authors supply an anonymous code link, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of well-known existing ingredients — token selection (as in LLMLingua/SelectiveContext), learned soft-token-style tuning with LoRA (as in ICAE/500xCompressor), and bidirectional attention for encoders (as in LLM2Vec/NV-Embed). No component is individually new, and the combination is fairly straightforward. The 'autoencoding-free' framing is the main selling point, but Table 5 shows the AE question is more nuanced than the paper's framing suggests.

Gains over the strongest baseline (EPL) are small and inconsistent: at 5x compression the average OOD improvement is only 0.77 F1 / 1.0 EM, and SAC actually underperforms EPL on several individual datasets (e.g., BioASQ at 5x). No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-seed results are reported, so many of the improvements—especially at 5x—may not be meaningful.

Scale of evaluation is narrow: experiments use only Llama-3.2-1B as both encoder and target LLM. There is no evidence the approach works with larger models or different model families, which weakens the generality claims. Contexts are limited to 510-token sub-contexts, so the claim of addressing 'extremely long contexts' is not really tested—no experiments on genuinely long-context settings where compression matters most.

Efficiency claims are under-supported: the paper motivates compression by inference latency and GPU memory savings, but reports no measured inference-time speedup, memory reduction, or end-to-end wall-clock comparison. Moreover, bidirectional attention over the full context during compression means the full context must still be processed at compression time; the practical cost profile of SAC vs. baselines is not quantified beyond training-time (Table 7).

A large gap remains between all compression methods and the uncompressed Full-FT baseline (e.g., 63.6 vs 71.5 F1 in-domain at 5x), which is acknowledged only implicitly; the paper does not discuss what information is lost or when compression is actually advisable.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., that SAC 'avoids any impairment to the language model's original language modeling capabilities' (the target LLM is frozen by design, so this is not a demonstrated property of the method), and the abstract emphasizes '1 EM improvement' which is a modest headline result.

Some writing/presentation issues: minor typos ('inferenece'), the causal/bidirectional attention modification is described loosely, and the interplay between the uniform (middle-token) selection strategy and the claimed 'semantic anchor' story is underdeveloped—the anchors are not actually selected for semantic importance by default, which sits awkwardly with the method's name and motivation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper challenges the necessity of autoencoding (AE) pretraining in context compression, and the 'anchor token' idea of deriving compressed representations from the context's own tokens is intuitive and elegant.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 12 QA datasets (6 in-domain, 6 out-of-domain), three compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), and fair re-training of all soft-compression baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL) on the same data.

Thorough ablation studies covering the two proposed components (bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings), token selection strategies, and the AE objective itself, including an interesting and honest observation that AE may not be essential even for 500xCompressor at high ratios.

Useful analysis beyond aggregate metrics: attention map visualizations, t-SNE analysis of Key/Value representation spaces, pretraining perplexity and training-time comparison (26-31% faster), and loss curves.

The method preserves the target LLM untouched (no target-model finetuning), consistent with the ICAE/500xCompressor setup, and the representation-alignment analysis gives a plausible mechanistic explanation for why anchor tokens work.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of known ingredients — token selection (from LLMLingua-style methods), KV-based compression carriers (500xCompressor), uniform positional anchoring (EPL), and bidirectional attention for encoders (LLM2Vec/NV-Embed). The technical contribution is an integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (EPL) at 5x compression are modest (e.g., +0.77 F1 in-domain average, and SAC actually loses to EPL on several individual OOD datasets such as BioASQ at 5x). Without statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seeds, some claimed advantages may be within noise.
Single model scale (Llama-3.2-1B) and a single encoder/target pairing; no evidence the gains transfer to larger or different LLMs, which weakens generality claims.

The anchor selection strategy is simplistic (middle token of uniform chunks) and largely inherited from EPL; while the Lingua-2 ablation is appreciated, there is no exploration of learned or adaptive selection, which seems the most natural avenue for this architecture.

Compression is applied per 510-token sub-context with concatenated representations; the interaction between chunking, loss of cross-chunk information, and effective compression ratio is not analyzed, and the gap to the Full-FT upper bound (e.g., 63.6 vs 71.5 F1 in-domain at 5x) remains substantial.

Reproducibility concerns: the anonymous code link in Section 7 appears to be missing/empty in the manuscript text; also minor writing issues (e.g., 'inferenece') and an incomplete sentence in Section 3.2.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether autoencoding pretraining is necessary for context compression, with a simple architectural answer (semantic anchor tokens + anchor embeddings + bidirectional encoder attention).

Comprehensive evaluation: in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA across 5x/15x/51x compression ratios, model scaling to 3B and 8B, long-context summarization (QMSum, GovReport) and 24K long-context QA, with baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, Activation Beacon, DAST) retrained under identical settings for fairness.

Useful ablations covering each component (bidirectional attention, anchor embedding), token selection strategies (random, Lingua-2, uniform), and the AE/LM objective interaction, plus training-efficiency and FLOPs/latency comparisons.

Thoughtful analysis section: AE-LM gradient cosine similarity, attention map visualizations, and KV-space t-SNE provide mechanistic insight into why anchor-based representations behave differently from special-token compressors.
Reproducibility statement with released data, model, and code; hyperparameters and detailed per-dataset results in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially a combination of known ideas — uniform/position-based token selection (from EPL/token-selection literature), learned embeddings added to existing tokens, bidirectional attention for representation learning (LLM2Vec, NV-Embed), and KV-based compression (500xCompressor). The contribution is more of a well-executed engineering combination than a fundamentally new technique.

Gains over the strongest baseline (EPL) are modest at low compression ratios (e.g., 63.63 vs 62.90 F1 at 5x in-domain); the advantage becomes meaningful mainly at 15x/51x, and no statistical significance tests or variance over seeds are reported for any comparison.

The anchor selection strategy is simplistic (middle token per chunk); there is limited investigation of smarter selection or learned selection, which weakens the 'semantic anchor' framing — the anchors are not demonstrably semantic beyond the uniform heuristic.

Evaluation scope is narrow: predominantly MRQA-style extractive QA plus two summarization datasets; no evaluation on generation-heavy, reasoning, or retrieval-augmented settings where information discarding by anchor selection could hurt more.

Some claims outrun the evidence: the assertion that AE capabilities 'conflict' with downstream requirements is supported mainly by gradient orthogonality on one setup, and the discussion of why EPL/SAC attention patterns differ is speculative ('hypothetically').
Several soft-compression baselines (e.g., ICAE) perform far below published numbers, raising concerns that baseline tuning may be suboptimal despite identical training settings.

Missing efficiency details for the practical deployment story: encoder still processes the full context with bidirectional attention at compression time, and KV-cache storage/training-memory overhead relative to baselines is not fully characterized beyond the 500xCompressor FLOPs comparison.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA splits, three model scales (1B/3B/8B), and long-context summarization (QMSum, GovReport) tasks.

Well-designed ablations covering each proposed component (anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention), token selection strategies, and the role of the autoencoding objective, including a convincing AE-vs-LM gradient cosine similarity analysis supporting the core hypothesis.
Additional analyses (attention maps, t-SNE of key/value representations, FLOPs and latency comparisons) provide reasonable mechanistic insight into why SAC outperforms prior soft-compression methods.
Reproducibility statement with released data, code, and detailed hyperparameters; training is faster than competing soft-compression baselines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of existing components — token selection from hard-compression methods (SelectiveContext/LLMLingua line), EPL's position layout, 500xCompressor's KV-based compressed representation, bidirectional attention as in LM2Vec/NV-Embed, and a learnable additive embedding (akin to prefix/prompt tuning). The paper's framing of 'a priori compression capability' oversells what amounts to EPL plus two modest architectural tweaks.

The central claim that autoencoding pretraining is misaligned and harmful rests mainly on the authors' own experiments (Table 5) and is contradicted in part by prior work (ICAE reports AE+LM helps); a broader, more rigorous validation across architectures/settings would be needed for this to be a strong general finding.

Gains over the strongest baseline (EPL) are modest (roughly 2-4 F1/EM points), and the ablation showing SAC(Random) still performs reasonably well suggests the improvements derive more from the architecture than from the claimed 'semantic anchor' selection, weakening the paper's central narrative.

Uneven baseline treatment: the hard-compression baseline (LLMLingua-2) is only evaluated at 5x, and the evaluation is restricted to the Llama model family and MRQA-derived datasets; generalization claims would benefit from broader benchmarks and stronger recent compression methods.

The bidirectional attention modification departs from the target LLM's causal pretraining, but there is limited analysis of the potential train/deploy mismatch or of when this change could hurt (e.g., the interplay between bidirectional encoding and causal decoding is asserted rather than deeply examined).

Writing at times leans on vague, argumentative language ('we believe', 'arguably', 'hypothetically') in place of precise analysis, and the contribution relative to EPL is acknowledged but not sharply delineated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: removing the autoencoding pretraining stage and deriving compressed representations directly from selected original-context 'anchor' tokens is a sensible, testable hypothesis, and the paper provides direct evidence for it (Table 5 ablations, AE/LM gradient cosine-similarity analysis in Fig. 9).

Comprehensive evaluation: in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA, three compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), three model scales (1B/3B/8B), long-context summarization (32K) and long-context QA (24K), with all soft-compression baselines retrained under identical settings for fairness.

Component ablations (anchor embedding, bidirectional attention), token-selection strategy ablations, and AE/LM objective ablations are all included and support the design choices; the finding that AE hurts even in 500xCompressor is an interesting, transferable insight for the field.

Practical efficiency analysis is a plus: training is ~26-31% faster than ICAE/500xCompressor, and the FLOP and empirical latency comparison (Tables 12-13) shows bidirectional attention does not introduce inference overhead.
The paper is clearly written with a clean formulation, and code/data/models are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
Consistent gains over the strongest baseline (EPL) across nearly all settings, with no sign of diminishing returns as model size grows.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is largely a combination of existing ingredients — uniform chunk-based token selection (from EPL), per-layer KV compression (from 500xCompressor), and bidirectional attention (well established for encoders/embeddings, e.g., LLM2Vec, NV-Embed). The main contribution is the observation that AE pretraining is unnecessary when compression tokens are real context tokens, which is valuable but arguably incremental.

The default anchor selection strategy (middle token of each fixed-size chunk) is simple and heuristic; Table 4 shows selection matters (random drops ~4 F1), yet the paper does not explore stronger learned or retrieval-based selection, leaving an obvious avenue for improvement unaddressed.

Compression quality still lags substantially behind the Full-FT uncompressed baseline (e.g., 54.95 vs 71.51 F1 at 15x), and at 51x SAC loses to EPL or 500x on several individual datasets; the paper averages over datasets, which can mask these per-dataset weaknesses.

Some analyses are qualitative and only suggestive rather than conclusive (attention-map interpretation, t-SNE key/value visualizations, 'arguably'/'hypothesis' framing in Sections 5.2-5.3); no quantitative metric ties the representation-closeness claims to downstream performance.
No statistical significance testing, variance over random seeds, or confidence intervals are reported, despite relatively modest margins over EPL on some OOD settings (e.g., +0.77 F1 at 5x).

Evaluation is limited to one model family (Llama-3.x) and mostly QA-style extractive tasks; ROUGE-1 F1 for QA evaluation (rather than standard token-level MRQA F1) and the small summarization gains (18.49 vs 17.61) leave some uncertainty about general applicability.

Details of the bidirectional-attention modification (how it interacts with RoPE/position IDs, causal-masking changes in a decoder-only model, and whether the decoder is kept strictly causal) are underspecified in the main text, which could hinder exact reproduction.
